The biggest obstacle I see to the adoption of electronic medical records is not really technological or cryptographic. As usual, any time money, politics and fear-mongering mix into the issue, nothing good or productive comes out of it.

Does the technology exist to securely encrypt and store medical records? Of course it does. Can patients be trusted to manage their keys or passwords and back-up regularly? Not so much. Not because they are not smart or “techie” enough, but because dealing with keys, backup keys, passwords and backup media require time and effort, which is not the convenience patients seek.

The idea of someone else storing your medical records is not necessarily new or unique. We trust banks with our money and our safety deposit boxes. We keep our excess belongings in self-storage units. We keep personal and financial information on online services. Medical records, in the practical sense, are the same. The services or locations holding our records can be accessed by us (the patients), and should be accessible by other healthcare providers, otherwise there is no point for all this high-tech migration. Seeing how all sorts of organizations suffer data breaches on a regular basis, there is no guarantee our medical data would not suffer the same fate. So what do we do then? We become sole holders of the password or key for decryption?

There are problems with that idea as well. What if we are incapacitated when we are admitted to a hospital? Or what if we lose the key (or key storage token, etc.) or cannot remember the password to save our lives (no pun intended)? Are our records lost in encryption for eternity?

Some people carry a USB bracelet or necklace with their medical records saved in unencrypted, easily shareable format (.jpg, .pdf). It is not feasible to carry these devices all the time, and there are times when we visit locations where we do not want to lose and expose our medical data.

If we “have an app for that”, which can open the medical record from the lock screen of a phone, it is effectively the same level of security as an unsecured USB drive. To increase security, can this app be set to contact loved ones and they can provide an access code to the records? A bit better security measure, but how do the loved ones verify that it is in fact an emergency medical person possessing the phone? In case of a delayed response, by the time someone gets back to the emergency services personnel, it may be too late for the data to be useful.

As far as easy accessibility by healthcare providers goes, this is where arguments that are not entirely technological come in. Do we want a massive national database with everyone's medical records in it? What if this giant repository suffers the same fate as databases at other breached organizations have? Who is to say law enforcement, surveillance agencies, or even government contractors (read: civilians) do not access the database and use it inappropriately? Can the agency responsible for maintaining the database be secretly compelled to share your records? Are there any legal and procedural safeguards in place to make sure nobody other than the patient can access the records without a court order? And if it is a national database, at what level of jurisdiction will the case be heard? Will the patient be allowed to contest the request for disclosure? What if someone simply “does not want to play”; he or she prefers not to have his or her records stored by an agency of a ruling body? Will that be considered automatically suspicious? Will participating be compulsory? If using the often-suggested escrow method, an escrow holder can still be compelled by a variety of means to cooperate with authorities, or with anyone else. To make matters possibly even worse, what if insurance companies, or just straight-out extortionists illegally get a hold of your data and use it against you?

Then there is politics injected into the argument. Big government versus small government, Uncle Sam getting into “states' business”, will the records be used to identify/profile/stereotype “possible” offenders, automatic review of records when someone applies for a public sector job...

On the money side of the issue, different record storage vendors will fight to force competitors out, so they will lock medical records to their own proprietary format, discouraging medical providers from switching platforms. Similar to big pharma style marketing, vendors may wine-and-dine medical providers to encourage them to use their product. Make no mistake: the patient will be the number one victim here.

When a patient uses the services of multiple healthcare providers, can they all maintain local copies of the records? That in itself is not a bad idea, especially if the record storage infrastructure is not connected to the Internet or other external network, but what are the guarantees of the office deleting the local copy when the patient transfers to another doctor?

The truth is that the idea of universal electronic medical records storage and access is not trustworthy enough yet. There are more questions and concerns than there are solid answers. We cannot afford to entrust our most personal information to incomplete platforms. As much as I am a proud geek--and generally an advocate of using technology for the greater good--I believe that medical records are among those “analog” entities that erode our privacy instead of strengthening it when we convert them to ones an zeros with currently available solutions.
